content: (Creating a discusion thread for #announce > Literate: Dual-purpose Lean & Markdown files )

Hi everyone,

I’m excited to share a new library I've been working on: Literate.

https://github.com/tani/literate

This library leverages Lean 4's powerful macro system to allow you to create files that are valid Markdown and valid Lean 4 code simultaneously, without needing an external preprocessor.

How it works

By using a custom parser, the library allows you to write prose directly in your .lean files. Only the code blocks (e.g., inside ~~~lean ... ~~~) are evaluated by the Lean kernel, while everything else is treated as ignored metadata/prose.

Lean

import Literate

# This heading is ignored by Lean but rendered by Markdown viewers

This line is prose and is also ignored.

~~~lean
namespace Demo

def success := "This was evaluated!"
#check success

end Demo
~~~

Why this?

We've seen amazing examples of polyglot literate programming in other ecosystems—Agda, for instance, has a long-standing tradition of beautiful literate files. I believe Lean 4's macro extensibility gives us a unique "competitive edge" to make literate programming even more seamless and native.

Future & Community

Currently, this is a personal project, but I’m wondering if there is interest in moving this to the leanprover-community organization in the future? I feel that having a standardized, built-in way to handle literate Lean would be a great asset for the community, especially for educational materials and documentation.

I'd love to hear your thoughts or feedback!

This sounds like a cool idea, but how does it compare to just writing markdown in comments? That's what Rocq does AFAIK.
Trying to render such a literate file as markdown doesn't seem to work very well:
render.png

Thanks! I wrote a very primitive macro, so I suspect that’s why it’s breaking. I’ll work on improving the quality of the macro. In principle, Lean and Markdown should be syntactically orthogonal, so I’d appreciate advice from the experts here—mainly regarding the macro implementation.
​Regarding the difference between this and writing Markdown inside comments: to process the latter as Markdown, you’d typically need to write a filter. The noteworthy point here—as is also the case with Agda—is that by implementing this at the macro level, we eliminate the need for an external filter altogether.

TANIGUCHI Masaya said:

we eliminate the need for an external filter altogether

The purpose of the screenshot above is to demonstrate that this is false. You can either have a valid Lean file or a valid markdown file, and the other direction requires filtering.

regarding the example where the rendering breaks: that's actually the correct behavior for Markdown, so it’s not a bug. However, I do think the error messages should be more helpful. Thanks for trying it out and showing me!
Also, I should point out that Verso similarly breaks when you input nested, malicious comment strings.
Regardless you have import Literate at the beginning of the rendered markdown
You can use indented codeblock :+1:

it should be a given that the macro works correctly for inputs that are valid as both Markdown and Lean. If the input is invalid in either Markdown or Lean, isn't it only natural that it wouldn't work? In fact, your code wouldn't even compile in Lean.

Incidentally, these ideas have already been put into practice in Agda and Common Lisp compilers. Given that many users have successfully overcome the concerns you’ve pointed out, I am confident that brilliant minds like yourselves will also be able to implement this.
With Markdown preview on the left, the State Panel on the right, and Lean code in the middle, I’ve finally achieved the ultimate editing environment.
What's the statut of this project, @TANIGUCHI Masaya ?

https://reservoir.lean-lang.org/@tani/LiterateLean

As you can see here, it's a very lightweight macro, so it builds perfectly fine even with the latest version. In fact, I continue to use this framework for my own work.

It's lightweight, visually clean as Markdown, and the LSP works flawlessly, so I have absolutely no complaints. That being said, if you have any feature requests, they are more than welcome!
Furthermore, since the early days of development, I have been utilizing AI to enhance the macro's implementation, making the overall system much more robust.
